title: The pot and the lid
hook: like a water pot turned upside down, nothing stays in; an upright pot fills

segments.voice: Yesterday: the desert travelers, and your line, just enough to cross. Did you stop at enough? Today closes a week, with a question about how we listen. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

Look back at this week. Girimananda's bedside. The nuns and the inspiring sign. Six ways to be dear. The old Buddha in the evening sun. Seven marks of a friend. The desert crossing. That's a lot of teaching in seven days. Now an honest question: how much of it stayed? The Book of Threes has a sutta for exactly that question. It sorts listeners into three kinds, using three homely pictures: a pot turned upside down, a lap full of snacks, and a pot standing the right way up. Today: avakujja.
screen: `A WEEK OF TEACHINGS.` → `HOW MUCH STAYED?` → `THREE KINDS OF LISTENER.`

segments.voice: The first listener goes often to hear the teaching. The teaching is good in the beginning, middle and end. But they don't attend to any of it, not while sitting, not after they get up. That person, the Buddha says, is like a pot turned upside down. Pour water on it, and it all runs off. The second listener follows while sitting. They get the beginning, the middle and the end. But once they stand up, it's gone. That one is like a person with sesame seeds and rice cakes in their lap, who forgets and stands up, and everything scatters on the ground. The third listener takes it in while sitting and still holds it after getting up. That one is like a pot standing upright. Pour water in, and it stays. So, about today's title: there is no lid in the sutta. There's an upside-down pot, a lap and an upright pot. The lid is our word, and it's a fair one. Plenty of us listen with a lid on: the phone in one hand, the reply already half-composed. Notice that the first two listeners aren't lazy. They show up. They sit through the whole thing. The difference is the angle of the pot. Turning it upright is something you can do: recall a teaching later, repeat it to someone, try it once. That's what the carry has been asking of you every day this week.
screen: `THE UPSIDE-DOWN POT.` · `THE LAP THAT SPILLS.` · `THE UPRIGHT POT.` · then, large: `KEEP THE POT UPRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen with an upright pot. Sit, and settle. Picture a clay pot resting in your lap, mouth up. Now, one at a time, let this week's lines pour in: ten perceptions. Inspired, then calm. Six ways to be dear. Even his. A friend gives the hard thing. Just enough to cross. Which ones stayed in? Which ran off? No grading. Pick the one that matters most to you, and hold it for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
avakujja. The Pali word for upside down, naming the first of three listeners in the Book of Threes: an upside-down pot, a spilling lap, and an upright pot that holds what's poured in. Today's word.
Your line: keep the pot upright. Today, next time someone tells you something that matters, repeat it back once, later in the day. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the three pots when encouraging students to review and practice what they hear, and in some communities Dhamma talks are followed by recitation or discussion to help the teaching stay.

fork.setup: you sat through the whole talk and followed it. but by the time you reached the door, it was gone. which listener are you?
fork.reveal: the lap: you held it while seated, then stood up and it scattered. the good news is the pot can be turned upright.

original.note: Pali avakujja: upside down, turned over; the sutta's name, for the pot that holds nothing.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you show up to the teaching, it sinks in.
what it means: AN 3.30 says some listeners sit through all of it and keep nothing; the pot must be upright.
what a scholar hears: the three are named for wisdom: 'upside-down wisdom,' 'lap wisdom' and 'wide wisdom.'

notes: AN 3.30 paraphrased. Confirm the lap items (sesame, rice, sweets/cakes) and the 'wide wisdom' (puthu-panna) naming.
The title's 'lid' isn't in the sutta; the script says so plainly. A Keeper may prefer to retitle the index ('the pot and the lap').
